paragraphs: BitsFusion tackles the storage and transfer costs of diffusion image generators. These models can produce high-quality images, but their many parameters make them cumbersome to distribute and use on devices with limited resources. The paper focuses on compressing the UNet component of Stable Diffusion v1.5 by representing its weights with substantially fewer bits.

The method combines several changes that address the loss of precision introduced by quantization. It assigns bit budgets to individual layers, improves the initialization of the compressed model, and changes training to reduce quantization error. These components treat compression as a coordinated modeling and training problem: the allocation of precision and the way the compressed model is trained both influence the resulting image quality.

The authors report a 1.99-bit weight representation and a model size reduction of 7.9 times. Across benchmark datasets and human evaluation, they also report better generation quality than the original model. For the evaluated Stable Diffusion component, the findings show that very aggressive weight compression can coexist with improved image quality, making storage savings more useful than a size reduction achieved at the expense of the output.
neurips-2024-bitsfusion-1-99-bits-weight.tldr: BitsFusion compresses Stable Diffusion v1.5’s UNet to 1.99-bit weights, reporting a 7.9-fold size reduction and improved generation quality.

paragraphs: Some neural networks make decisions through layers that solve an optimization problem. Training the whole network requires propagating gradients through that solution. This becomes expensive when the problem contains many variables or constraints, because existing implicit differentiation methods can require costly operations involving Jacobian matrices. BPQP addresses this computational bottleneck in differentiable convex optimization.

The framework uses the structure of the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker matrix, which arises from the optimization problem’s optimality conditions, to reorganize the backward computation. It expresses that computation as a simpler, decoupled quadratic program. This makes first-order optimization algorithms available for calculating the required gradients and creates a route for incorporating advances in optimization solvers.

Experiments on simulated and real-world data report overall execution times typically about an order of magnitude faster than other differentiable optimization layers. The contribution concerns the efficiency of the complete learning pipeline, since the reported gains extend beyond an isolated matrix operation. Its solver-oriented formulation also offers the possibility of further efficiency improvements as compatible solver technology develops.
neurips-2024-bpqp-a-differentiable-conve.tldr: BPQP turns differentiation through convex optimization layers into a simpler quadratic program, reporting roughly tenfold overall speedups in its experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover hidden causal factors and changing dynamics from temporal sequences whose statistical behavior varies over time. Existing approaches require either observing the variables that describe the domain or placing a Markov assumption on those variables. Such requirements become restrictive when the relevant domain information is unavailable.

The authors instead adopt a sparse transition assumption and investigate when changes in the transitions contain enough information to identify distribution shifts. Their theoretical contribution gives identifiability results under conditions on the significance of that variability. The guarantee therefore depends on the structure and informativeness of the transitions, rather than simply on having a sequence of observations.

Building on this analysis, the paper introduces CtrlNS, a framework that combines transition sparsity with conditional independence constraints to identify distribution changes and latent factors. Experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets report substantial improvements over existing baselines. The work offers a different set of assumptions for learning temporal causal representations, with theoretical conditions explaining when that alternative can support identification.
neurips-2024-causal-temporal-representat.tldr: CtrlNS uses sparse transitions and conditional independence to identify changing distributions and hidden temporal factors under stated identifiability conditions.

paragraphs: CoMERA targets the computing and memory costs of training large AI models. Its approach keeps model parameters in tensor-compressed form during training and adapts their ranks through a multi-objective optimization formulation. Adjusting rank provides a way to balance compression with the model’s ability to retain accuracy throughout training.

Compression alone can introduce computational overhead, so the paper also improves the numerical operations and GPU implementation used for tensorized training. These changes include optimized tensorized embeddings and tensor-vector contractions. The combination matters because a compact representation becomes more practical when operating on it also reduces training time.

The authors report training epochs that are two to three times faster than standard training. In a tested six-encoder transformer with single-batch training, CoMERA is twice as fast and nine times more memory-efficient than GaLore. On a BERT-like code-generation language model, it achieves approximately twice the pretraining speed and 4.23-fold compression. The authors suggest that further high-performance computing optimization may extend pretraining cost reductions to other large language models.
neurips-2024-comera-computing-and-memory.tldr: CoMERA combines adaptive tensor compression with optimized GPU computation to reduce training memory and time while retaining strong accuracy.

paragraphs: Estimating the consequences of an intervention becomes difficult when a causal graph contains high-dimensional variables such as images. Existing identification algorithms often depend on conditional likelihoods, which can be hard to estimate for such data. Unobserved confounders add another challenge when trying to generate samples from an intervention’s outcome distribution.

The paper shows how conditional generative models can produce samples from any identifiable interventional distribution for a given causal graph. Its algorithm follows the recursive structure of existing likelihood-based identification procedures, trains a collection of feed-forward models, and connects their computations to generate the desired samples. Identifiability remains an essential condition: the construction supplies a sampling procedure for effects that the causal structure allows observational data to identify.

The authors demonstrate image-to-image intervention sampling on Colored MNIST, analyze spurious feature correlations in generative models pretrained on CelebA, and generate intervention samples involving text and images from MIMIC-CXR. These examples illustrate how the theoretical construction can support causal analysis when the variables themselves are rich, high-dimensional objects.
neurips-2024-conditional-generative-mode.tldr: The paper shows how to compose conditional generative models to sample from any identifiable interventional distribution for a given causal graph.

paragraphs: This paper examines repeated contracts when the agent responds through a learning algorithm that achieves no-regret outcomes. The principal chooses contractual incentives while the agent learns how to act over repeated interactions. This setting reflects the possibility that participants manage uncertainty through learning instead of implementing complicated dynamic strategies.

For the canonical case in which actions lead to success or failure, the authors establish a simple optimal policy for the principal. It begins with a linear contract using a positive scalar and later switches that scalar to zero. Following the switch, the agent’s learning behavior moves through its action space in a way that can continue producing rewards for the principal without payment costs.

The welfare consequences are more varied than the payment reduction alone suggests: the authors show instances in which both participants benefit relative to the best static contract. They also extend their analysis to general linearly-scaled contracts and uncertainty about the interaction horizon. The results show why the agent’s learning dynamics can materially change which repeated contracts are advantageous.
neurips-2024-contracting-with-a-learning.tldr: For a canonical repeated-contract setting with a no-regret learning agent, an optimal principal strategy pays initially and then switches to zero payments.

paragraphs: This paper studies which loss-minimizing solutions training selects in deep linear networks for univariate regression. It measures sharpness using the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian, a quantity describing curvature around a solution. Although minimizers can be arbitrarily sharp, the authors prove that their sharpness cannot fall below a bound that increases linearly with network depth.

The central result concerns gradient flow, the limiting training dynamics of gradient descent as the learning rate vanishes. Under the studied initializations, gradient flow reaches a minimizer whose sharpness is at most a constant multiple of that lower bound. The constant depends on the conditioning of the data covariance matrix, but does not grow with network width or depth.

This provides a precise sense in which training implicitly favors relatively flat solutions. For small-scale initialization, the learned weight matrices are approximately rank-one and have aligned singular vectors. For residual initialization, the authors prove gradient-flow convergence with Gaussian initialization. Numerical experiments illustrate the theory and connect it to gradient descent with a non-vanishing learning rate.
neurips-2024-deep-linear-networks-for-re.tldr: Under the studied initializations, gradient flow in deep linear regression networks selects minima within a data-dependent constant factor of the sharpness lower bound.

paragraphs: DevBench provides a way to compare vision–language models with human language learning. The motivation is that models trained on smaller amounts of naturalistic, multimodal data are often assessed using adult-level benchmarks. Those evaluations can cover a narrow set of abilities and lack direct comparisons with how children and adults actually respond.

The benchmark contains seven tasks covering word knowledge, syntax, and meaning, together with behavioral data from children and adults. Its comparisons focus on response patterns rather than absolute performance. This makes the benchmark useful for examining whether a model’s behavior resembles human behavior across the tested language abilities, alongside measuring whether its answers are successful.

The evaluated models vary in how closely they match human response patterns across tasks. Better task performance is also associated with greater behavioral similarity. Following OpenCLIP through training, the authors find that additional training brings its responses closer to adult patterns. These findings make developmental comparisons more concrete and expose differences between model and human language learning that can guide future model improvements.
neurips-2024-devbench-a-multimodal-devel.tldr: DevBench compares vision–language models with children and adults across seven language tasks using their patterns of responses.

paragraphs: DIVA addresses the challenge of creating enough diverse simulated tasks to train agents that can adapt after a few experiences. Meta-reinforcement learning seeks this adaptation ability, but learning it still requires substantial training diversity. In complex simulators, manually designing tasks is costly, and changing simulator parameters does not necessarily produce meaningful differences between tasks.

The paper proposes an evolutionary task-generation approach that can work with arbitrary simulator parameterizations while incorporating available domain knowledge. This combines the flexibility of unsupervised environment design with some of the structure used by domain randomization and procedural generation. The intended benefit is to make useful task diversity accessible even when a simulator’s parameters are difficult to organize into a well-designed task generator.

The reported experiments show that DIVA handles complex parameterizations and trains adaptive agent behavior while substantially outperforming competitive prior baselines. The authors describe this combination of flexible generation and domain guidance as semi-supervised environment design. Their findings support its potential for training more capable adaptive agents in realistic simulated domains.
neurips-2024-enabling-adaptive-agent-tra.tldr: DIVA uses evolutionary task generation and available domain knowledge to train adaptive agents in complex simulators.

paragraphs: NATURAL investigates whether observational text can support causal effect estimation without the usual amount of manual data collection and structuring. The aim is to estimate the consequences of interventions from large, diverse text datasets. The approach depends on appropriate causal assumptions, which remain necessary for interpreting the resulting estimates as intervention effects.

The proposed estimators use language models to supply conditional distributions over variables of interest given the text. These distributions assist the computation of classical causal effect estimators. The pipeline also automates data curation and uses language models to impute missing information, bringing several steps of turning unstructured accounts into usable evidence into one estimation process.

The authors evaluate the pipeline using six observational datasets, including two synthetic and four real datasets, paired with randomized-trial ground truth. Their effect estimates fall within three percentage points of the corresponding ground truth, including for real Phase 3/4 clinical trials. The results suggest that text can contain useful causal information and support further development of automated estimation pipelines under suitable assumptions.
neurips-2024-end-to-end-causal-effect-es.tldr: NATURAL combines language-model distributions with classical causal estimators to estimate intervention effects from unstructured text under appropriate causal assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies minimizing a convex objective when the constraints are themselves strongly convex functions. Such constraints have additional curvature, but the previously best complexity guarantee did not benefit from that structure. The authors ask whether the constraint curvature can be used to reach a desired accuracy with fewer optimization steps.

They develop accelerated primal-dual algorithms that progressively estimate the strong convexity of the Lagrangian, the function combining the objective and constraints. This allows the methods to exploit curvature supplied by the constraints. The resulting complexity improves from order one over the target accuracy to order one over its square root. The authors establish order-optimality through a matching lower bound for strongly-convex-concave saddle point optimization.

The paper also reports improved performance on sparsity-inducing constrained problems, including Google’s personalized PageRank problem. A restarted version of the method identifies the optimal solution’s sparsity pattern within finitely many steps. Together, these results connect faster convergence guarantees with the ability to determine which components of a sparse solution should be active.
neurips-2024-faster-accelerated-first-or.tldr: New accelerated primal-dual methods exploit strongly convex constraints to improve complexity from O(1/ε) to the order-optimal O(1/√ε).

paragraphs: HOI-Swap edits videos by replacing an object with one specified in a reference image, focusing on objects handled by people. This requires more than changing the object’s appearance. When its shape or function changes, the hand’s interaction may also need to change for the edited scene to remain believable.

The framework uses self-supervised training and divides editing into two stages. First, it swaps the object in a single frame while adjusting interaction details such as the grasp to reflect the replacement object’s properties. Second, it carries that edit through the video. To control alignment with the original motion, it warps a sequence from the edited frame using sampled motion points, then conditions video generation on that warped sequence.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations report substantial improvements over existing methods, producing high-quality edits with realistic hand–object interactions. The two-stage design connects local interaction editing with sequence-level motion control. Its significance is that the replacement object and the hand’s behavior are treated as related parts of the same edit.
neurips-2024-hoi-swap-swapping-objects-i.tldr: HOI-Swap replaces objects in videos while adapting hand interactions and using motion-guided generation to extend the edit across frames.

paragraphs: This paper studies how language agents can choose discussion tactics strategically in One Night Ultimate Werewolf. The game involves uncertainty about players’ roles, including possible role changes, making conversation an important part of decision-making. The authors focus on controlling discussion tactics, an aspect that can receive limited attention in agents built around language models.

They first establish the existence of Perfect Bayesian Equilibria in two game scenarios, one allowing discussion and one without it. The analysis shows that discussion can substantially change players’ utilities by changing their beliefs. This provides a game-theoretic motivation for explicitly learning how to discuss, since conversational choices can alter the information on which later decisions depend.

Guided by that analysis, the authors introduce a language-agent framework instructed by a discussion policy trained with reinforcement learning. The policy determines which discussion tactics the agent should adopt. Experiments across several game settings demonstrate effectiveness and generalizability. The work connects strategic analysis with a learned mechanism for directing an agent’s conversational behavior.
neurips-2024-learning-to-discuss-strateg.tldr: The paper uses game-theoretic analysis and reinforcement learning to equip language agents with strategic discussion policies for One Night Ultimate Werewolf.

paragraphs: Lexicon3D investigates which visual foundation encoders are useful for understanding complex three-dimensional scenes. Scene encoding determines the visual information available to later tasks, but the best choices across different scenarios remain unclear. The paper addresses this through a comparative study of seven encoders drawn from image, video, and 3D foundation models.

The evaluation covers vision-language scene reasoning, visual grounding, segmentation, and registration. These tasks test different aspects of scene understanding, allowing the authors to examine whether an encoder’s strengths carry across uses. They find that unsupervised image models perform best overall, video models excel at object-level tasks, and diffusion models are beneficial for geometric tasks.

The study also finds unexpected limitations for language-pretrained encoders on language-related tasks. Combining visual experts through the MoVE strategy produces consistent performance improvements in the evaluation. These findings support selecting encoders according to the demands of a scene-understanding task and exploring combinations of their strengths, rather than assuming that a model’s pretraining category alone predicts its suitability.
neurips-2024-lexicon3d-probing-visual-fo.tldr: Lexicon3D compares seven visual encoders across four 3D scene tasks, finding task-specific strengths and consistent gains from combining visual experts.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a greedy algorithm can perform efficiently in a linear contextual bandit problem without explicit exploration. Such an algorithm chooses according to its current estimates, so its learning depends on the information provided by the contexts and selected actions. The central contribution is a distributional condition called Local Anti-Concentration, or LAC, under which this approach has a strong performance guarantee.

The authors show that LAC holds for a broad collection of distributions, including Gaussian, exponential, uniform, Cauchy, and Student’s t distributions, as well as other exponential-family distributions and truncated variants. This expands the range of distributional settings covered by theory for efficient greedy bandit learning.

Under the LAC condition, the cumulative expected regret is bounded by a polynomial in the logarithm of the time horizon. This is a sharper conclusion than merely showing sublinear growth. The result supplies a sufficient condition for efficient exploration-free behavior and clarifies how properties of the context distribution can support the greedy algorithm’s learning.
neurips-2024-local-anti-concentration-cl.tldr: A new Local Anti-Concentration condition gives greedy linear contextual bandits a polylogarithmic expected-regret guarantee across a broad class of distributions.

paragraphs: This paper examines what happens when a language model receives hundreds or thousands of examples in its prompt. In-context learning uses these examples at inference time without changing model weights. With larger context windows making this regime possible, the authors observe substantial gains over few-shot prompting across a variety of generative and discriminative tasks.

Obtaining enough human-written outputs can limit this approach, so the paper explores two alternatives. Reinforced ICL uses model-generated reasoning rationales in place of human rationales. Unsupervised ICL supplies domain-specific inputs without rationales. Both can be effective with many examples, particularly on complex reasoning tasks, suggesting that useful prompt material need not always take the form of human-produced worked solutions.

The experiments also show many-shot learning overriding pretraining biases, learning high-dimensional functions with numerical inputs, and performing comparably to supervised fine-tuning. These are observed capabilities in the studied settings. Finally, the paper finds that next-token prediction loss has limitations as a proxy for downstream in-context performance, making direct task evaluation important for understanding these gains.
neurips-2024-many-shot-in-context-learni.tldr: Hundreds or thousands of prompt examples improve in-context learning across tested tasks, with effective alternatives to relying entirely on human-written rationales.

paragraphs: Orchid is a sequence-modeling architecture designed to address the quadratic computational growth of traditional attention. It aims to retain the ability to capture long-range dependencies and perform in-context learning while scaling more efficiently to long inputs. Its central component is a global convolution whose kernel changes according to the input sequence.

A dedicated conditioning neural network constructs this input-dependent kernel. The authors design two simple conditioning networks that preserve shift equivariance in the convolution operation. This gives the architecture a structured way to adapt its computation to context while maintaining quasilinear scaling. The input-dependent kernel is the mechanism intended to combine expressive sequence processing with computational efficiency.

The paper evaluates Orchid on language modeling and image classification. In those experiments, it outperforms attention-based architectures including BERT and Vision Transformers while using smaller models. It also supports sequence lengths beyond the feasible limits of dense attention layers. These findings provide empirical support for adaptive global convolution as a practical architecture for efficient sequence modeling across multiple domains.
neurips-2024-orchid-flexible-and-data-de.tldr: Orchid uses input-dependent global convolution to achieve quasilinear sequence scaling and reports gains over attention-based models in language and image tasks.

paragraphs: Federated learning tries to exploit common structure across distributed client datasets, but differences between clients can make a single global model difficult to train reliably. Personalized federated learning addresses this by tailoring models to individual clients. A common strategy shares a learned representation while giving each client its own classifier.

The paper identifies a difficulty in learning those personalized classifiers: limited local data can make generalization challenging, while more elaborate remedies may be expensive. Its proposed approach frames representation learning as generative modeling, training representations with a classifier based on the global feature distribution. The pFedFDA algorithm then adapts global generative classifiers to the feature distributions of individual clients.

This creates a direct link between shared distributional information and local personalization. The global model supplies information learned across clients, while adaptation accounts for each client’s particular feature distribution. Extensive computer vision experiments report improved handling of complex distribution shifts and substantial gains over current state-of-the-art methods when data are scarce. The findings support feature-distribution adaptation as an efficient route to personalized models.
neurips-2024-personalized-federated-lear.tldr: pFedFDA personalizes federated models by adapting global generative classifiers to local feature distributions, with strong reported gains in data-scarce settings.

paragraphs: PINNacle provides a common testing framework for physics-informed neural networks used to solve partial differential equations. Although many PINN methods have been developed, their performance has lacked a broad, systematic comparison across different equations. The benchmark addresses that gap by putting varied problems and methods into a shared evaluation setting.

Its dataset includes more than twenty distinct PDEs spanning heat conduction, fluid dynamics, biology, and electromagnetics. The problems incorporate challenges such as complicated geometry, behavior at multiple scales, nonlinearity, and high dimensionality. A toolbox containing about ten state-of-the-art PINN methods supports systematic comparisons across this range, making it possible to examine how methods behave under different kinds of difficulty.

The authors conduct extensive experiments and analyze the methods’ strengths and weaknesses. Their discussion points toward research on domain decomposition and loss reweighting for problems involving multiple scales and complex geometry. PINNacle’s contribution is therefore both an evaluation resource and an analysis of where existing approaches need improvement, helping connect future method development to a wider range of PDE challenges.
neurips-2024-pinnacle-a-comprehensive-be.tldr: PINNacle benchmarks about ten physics-informed neural network methods on more than twenty diverse PDEs and analyzes their strengths and weaknesses.

paragraphs: This paper gives a theoretical explanation for how pretraining can reduce the number of examples a transformer needs in a test prompt. It moves beyond linear target functions, where earlier analyses did not demonstrate an advantage over directly solving regression from the prompt. The studied targets are nonlinear single-index functions: each applies a nonlinear link function to a projection of the input.

The key structural assumption is that the projection directions come from an r-dimensional subspace of a larger d-dimensional input space. The authors show that a transformer with a nonlinear MLP layer, trained by gradient descent, can learn these targets in context using prompt lengths that depend only on r. Its pretraining sample requirement depends on the information exponent of the link functions.

In contrast, algorithms learning the target directly from the test prompt have statistical complexity that scales with d in the studied setting. The result identifies a concrete benefit of pretraining: learning shared low-dimensional structure can make later tasks require fewer examples. This provides a nonlinear setting with a provable statistical advantage for in-context learning.
neurips-2024-pretrained-transformer-effi.tldr: For a structured nonlinear function class, pretraining lets a transformer’s required prompt length depend on intrinsic dimension rather than ambient input dimension.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when transition probabilities follow a multinomial logistic model with unknown parameters and known state–action features. The setting uses finite-length episodes and allows transitions to vary across steps within an episode. The objective is to explore efficiently while controlling regret, the accumulated cost of learning instead of acting optimally.

The first algorithm, RRL-MNL, uses randomized optimistic sampling so that its estimated value function is optimistic often enough to support a regret guarantee. Its bound grows with the square root of total interaction steps, and the paper establishes constant-time computational cost per episode. However, the bound also multiplies this growth by the inverse of a problem-dependent constant, κ, which can be large.

The second algorithm, ORRL-MNL, uses local gradient information from the transition model to improve that dependence. Its inverse-κ contribution becomes an additive term rather than multiplying the leading square-root growth term. The authors establish statistical and computational efficiency for both methods and report superior numerical performance. The main advance is combining randomized exploration with stronger efficiency guarantees for this transition model.
neurips-2024-randomized-exploration-for-.tldr: Two randomized exploration algorithms provide efficient learning guarantees for multinomial-logistic transition models, with the second improving dependence on a potentially large problem constant.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a zero-shot model aims to improve performance on the target data while preserving accuracy when the data distribution changes. Combining zero-shot and fine-tuned predictions can help, but the authors find that a single mixing coefficient reaches its best in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy at different values. Choosing one compromise can therefore sacrifice performance on the other.

Variance Reduction Fine-tuning, or VRF, changes the mixture for each test sample. It first collects training examples that the zero-shot model predicts incorrectly into a Zero-Shot Failure set. A test sample closer to that set receives more weight from the fine-tuned model. This uses the locations of known zero-shot failures to guide which model should contribute more to each prediction.

On ImageNet and five derived distribution shifts, VRF improves out-of-distribution accuracy by 1.5–2.0 percentage points over ensemble baselines while maintaining or increasing in-distribution accuracy. Other distribution-shift benchmarks show gains of 0.9–3.1 points. The authors explain the method through reduced prediction variance and residual error, supporting adaptive mixing as a way to improve both objectives in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-robust-fine-tuning-of-zero-.tldr: VRF adjusts zero-shot and fine-tuned prediction weights per sample using proximity to known zero-shot failures, improving robustness without sacrificing tested in-distribution accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies reconstructing a geometric configuration from distances between selected pairs of points. Such reconstruction appears in several machine-learning settings, and the authors focus on recovering the geometry from very few observed distances. They formulate the task through continuous, non-convex rank minimization and develop a variant of iteratively reweighted least squares.

The theoretical result gives a local convergence guarantee when a minimal random set of distance observations is available. Local convergence is the scope of the guarantee, so the theorem concerns behavior near a solution. A supporting result establishes a restricted isometry property for random distance measurements on a tangent space of the manifold of symmetric rank-r matrices. The authors suggest this tool could also aid analysis of other non-convex methods.

Experiments with simulated and real-world data compare reconstruction algorithms in terms of data efficiency, scalability, and generalizability. The proposed algorithm recovers the underlying geometry from fewer distance samples than state-of-the-art alternatives in these evaluations. The paper thus connects a conditional convergence analysis with empirical evidence of more economical use of distance information.
neurips-2024-sample-efficient-geometry-r.tldr: A non-convex, reweighted least-squares method reconstructs geometry from sparse distance observations, with a local convergence guarantee and reported sample-efficiency gains.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning reduces labeling effort by training from labels for groups of instances, called bags. In medical imaging, the desired output can include both a classification for the whole bag and localization predictions for individual instances. The paper addresses the gap between strong bag-level classification and comparatively weaker instance-level localization in existing methods.

The authors build a local-dependency mechanism around the observation that neighboring instances are likely to share a label. This explicitly brings a relationship between nearby instances into the model. The mechanism is flexible: it can operate on its own or be combined with approaches that capture global dependencies, including transformers. That flexibility allows local information to complement broader relationships among instances.

Extensive empirical validation reports state-of-the-art localization while retaining classification performance that is competitive with or better than alternatives. The contribution makes instance-level behavior a direct design concern in a setting trained only with bag labels. Its results show that modeling local dependencies can improve the usefulness of localization predictions without requiring a reported sacrifice in classification quality.
neurips-2024-sm-enhanced-localization-in.tldr: Sm models local relationships between neighboring instances to improve medical-image localization while preserving strong bag-level classification.

paragraphs: TrajCLIP predicts pedestrian trajectories in settings where movement depends on the scene, nearby people, and individual intentions. The authors argue that earlier approaches underuse similarities between past and future trajectories when modeling their feature spaces. Their method makes that relationship an explicit part of representation learning.

Historical and future trajectories are paired, encoded, and trained with a contrastive objective that enforces consistency within a shared feature space. The model also uses idempotent generative networks, with idempotent and tightness losses designed to control excessive expansion of the latent space. These components address both the relationship between observed and future motion and the complexity of the distribution being modeled.

The paper additionally introduces trajectory interpolation and synthetic trajectory data to strengthen model capacity and generalization. On public datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art prediction performance, along with strong results in transfer between scenes, transfer with few examples, and online learning. The findings support combining shared trajectory representations, latent-space constraints, and added trajectory data to improve prediction across these evaluated learning settings.
neurips-2024-trajclip-pedestrian-traject.tldr: TrajCLIP combines contrastive past–future alignment, constrained latent modeling, and synthetic trajectories to improve pedestrian prediction and transfer.
